topic: what are our app packaging options is unity an option for us with html assets, is electron or taurior something else an option

areas.name: What feels wrong with a browser tab today
areas.brief: Decided: every pain applies, but reach drives the choice. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Which platforms and stores the game must reach
areas.brief: Decided: Steam, macOS, Linux, and touch later are targets; Steam is someday; touch does not shape the choice now. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Install, trust, and updates
areas.brief: Decided: the app updates itself; signing comes later on both systems; the Mac app ships unsigned with steps to allow it; saves stay in today’s folder. Core: all three. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Stay in the browser, but make it feel like an app
areas.brief: Decided: a browser app window or an installable web app is off the list. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A thin shell on the system web view (Tauri and similar)
areas.brief: Decided: lean to Tauri 2. Core: lean Tauri. Open: confirm Tauri with a trial against the three proofs. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A shell that ships its own browser (Electron and similar)
areas.brief: Decided: Electron is the fallback, with one browser and one test tool, but a large download and no touch. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A game engine as the host (Unity, Godot)
areas.brief: Decided: Unity, Godot, and Bevy are off the list; 3D is a wish. Scope: kept.

areas.name: How the engine and the page talk inside a package
areas.brief: Decided: one engine interface with two paths. Core: two paths and the same stream on both. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Testing and iteration speed
areas.brief: Decided: the full suite inside the app on every system. Core: the full suite and the three proofs. Open: the macOS build needs a Mac and an Apple account. Scope: kept.

areas.name: A crash inside the app
areas.brief: Decided: direct calls stay, and engine errors are caught at the boundary with a restart from the last stoppage. Core. Risk: a hard crash still closes the app. Scope: kept.

areas.name: One match per start
areas.brief: Decided: playing again without a restart waits for the season layer. Core. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Builds and test runs on three systems
areas.brief: Decided: local builds for Windows and Linux now, hosted CI later; the first trial proves Windows and Linux, and the Mac proof comes later. Core. Scope: kept.

areas.name: Replay files open the app
areas.brief: Decided: the app registers the replay file type. Core. Scope: kept.

items.text: The installed game starts the engine, serves the page, and opens it in the player's default browser; each start plays one match.
The page reaches the engine over a WebSocket on 127.0.0.1, and the engine serves the page itself with cross-origin isolation headers.
The Windows setup file is about 2.6 MB and is not signed, so SmartScreen warns before it runs.
The product constraints say plain HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, MIT- or Apache-compatible dependencies only, and Windows 11 first as a browser page served by a local engine process.
Installers and packaging for other operating systems were deferred as a named later piece of work in the match engine workflow.
The existing HTML page stays the user interface, whatever the package is.
A Unity host pulls against the rule of permissive-licence dependencies only, and Unity does not render HTML without a separate web view plugin.
The browser chrome makes the game feel like a website.
A closed tab or a browser crash ends the match while the engine keeps running.
The default browser can be any browser at any version.
The tab is tolerable; the push comes from stores, trust, and other platforms.
The game must be able to ship on Steam.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: The game must run on macOS and Linux desktops as well as Windows.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: A tablet or phone is a real future target.
items.why: Chosen as a target in the first batch.

items.text: A touch target later pulls against shells that build for desktops only, such as Electron.
Reach to stores and platforms drives the package choice, not the pains of the browser tab.
items.why: Chosen as the top pain; the tab itself is tolerable.

items.text: Steam is a wish for someday, not a plan.
items.why: Chosen for Steam timing.
items.accepted-risk: A package chosen without Steam in mind can mean a second package when Steam comes.

items.text: Touch does not shape the package choice now; repackage when touch comes.
items.why: Touch is far enough away.
items.accepted-risk: A desktop-only shell means a second shell when touch comes.

items.text: All four readings hold at once: a Mac and Linux build, trust and install, one choice that grows to Steam and touch, and a richer view later.
The browser-tab release already ships for Linux, and a Mac build needs Apple signing and notarization whichever shell is chosen.
Unity came up for a 3D match view someday.
Unity came up because most games use it.
Unity came up to rule it in or out.
The product names the Football Manager 3D view as an anti-reference, because cluttered overlays hide the play.
A 3D view can live in the page itself with WebGL and a permissive library, with no game engine host.
The next release delivers one app window that can later grow to Steam and touch, before a Mac build, a signed install, or a richer view.
items.why: Chosen as the one thing the next release delivers.
items.accepted-risk: The next release adds repackaging work with no new player feature, and the unsigned-setup warning stays.

items.text: A 3D view is a someday wish and does not weigh on the package now.
items.why: Chosen for what 3D means for the game.

items.text: Unity stays a full candidate beside the web shells.
items.why: Chosen for the Unity verdict.
items.accepted-risk: With 3D only a wish, Unity keeps its costs (a licence exception to the product rules and a rebuilt interface or a web view plugin) without its main reason.

items.text: The comparison list is Tauri 2, Electron, Godot or Bevy, and Unity.
items.why: Chosen from the kinds of host.

items.text: A chromeless browser app window or an installable web app is off the list.
items.why: Not chosen; it has no store path.

items.text: Inside the package, the page calls the engine directly in the same program instead of over the local socket.
items.why: Chosen for the engine link.
items.accepted-risk: The page transport is rewritten and tied to one shell, and the browser test suite and replay viewing, which run over the socket today, need their own path.

items.text: The browser test suite drives the page against a live engine it starts, over the local socket.
Direct engine calls in the shell pull against the browser suite and replay viewing, which need the socket path.
A direct call means something different in each host: a Rust command in Tauri, a Node native addon in Electron, a native plugin in Unity, and a rewrite of the page in Godot or Bevy.
The person asked how the choices affect the ability to test and iterate easily, in answer to the summary check.
The official Tauri WebDriver runs on Windows and Linux only; macOS needs WebdriverIO with an embedded plugin or a paid driver.
Our Playwright suite can drive the page in a Tauri window on Windows through the WebView2 debugging port.
Tauri ships mocks for its engine calls, so page unit tests can run with no app window.
Tauri development mode reloads the page on a change and rebuilds the Rust side on a change.
Playwright drives Electron apps directly, but that support is still marked experimental.
An Electron installer is usually about 50 to 150 MB.
A Tauri app on Windows can be under 1 MB, plus about 1.8 MB when the WebView2 bootstrapper is embedded.
Tauri uses a different web engine on each system (WebView2, WKWebView, WebKitGTK), so the page needs testing on all three.
The Steam overlay does not draw over WebView2; a Tauri plugin adds a surface for the overlay as a workaround.
The Steam overlay works in Electron with extra flags and a steady repaint; Vampire Survivors first shipped on Electron.
The main Unity plugin that shows HTML (Vuplex 3D WebView) is paid per platform and has no Linux build.
Unity Personal is free up to 200,000 dollars of revenue; the runtime fee is cancelled; the runtime stays proprietary.
Rebuilding the page in Godot, Bevy, or Unity loses the Playwright suite and the page unit tests, because no browser automation reaches an engine-drawn interface.
A permissive Godot plugin shows a system web view on desktops only; mobile is only planned.
Unity with its HTML plugin pulls against the Linux target, because the plugin has no Linux build.
Direct engine calls only pull against keeping the page tests, which need the page to run in a plain browser over the socket.
One transport interface with two paths: direct engine calls in the app window, and the socket in a plain browser for tests, development, and replays.
items.why: Most page tests survive only if the page still runs in a plain browser over the socket.
items.accepted-risk: Two transport paths must stay equal, and a bug can live in one path only.

items.text: The whole browser suite also runs inside the packaged app on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
items.why: Chosen for app tests.
items.accepted-risk: With Tauri this needs a second test tool on Linux and macOS, and it gives the slowest test runs.

items.text: Unity, Godot, and Bevy leave the list; the comparison is Tauri 2 against Electron.
items.why: The Unity HTML plugin has no Linux build, and a rebuilt page loses every page test.

items.text: The full suite in the app on every system favours Electron, while size, touch later, and a Rust-native engine link favour Tauri.
The choice leans to Tauri 2 over Electron.
items.why: Installer size, a path to touch, and direct calls into the Rust engine with no Node addon.
items.accepted-risk: A second test tool on Linux and macOS, web engine differences between systems, and a workaround for the Steam overlay.

items.text: The first trial or release must show a full match playing in the app window on Windows, Linux, and macOS.
items.accepted-risk: The macOS part needs a Mac to build on and an Apple developer account, which the project does not have yet.

items.text: At least one full browser-suite test must pass inside the app on each system.
One match must give the same event stream over direct calls and over the socket.
A Windows installer near today size was not chosen as a proof.
Is Tauri 2 confirmed as the shell, and does a trial against the three proofs settle it?
The match engine workflow has a finished distribution piece that built the NSIS setup file and the Linux archive; an app shell changes it.
The finished distribution piece of the match engine workflow needs an update for the app shell.
The app checks for a new version and installs it itself.
items.why: Chosen for updates.
items.accepted-risk: A host for update files and an update signing key that must stay safe; a lost key strands every installed copy on its version.

items.text: Code signing comes later on both Windows and macOS, when the game has players.
items.why: Chosen for signing.
items.accepted-risk: Windows keeps the SmartScreen and antivirus warnings, and on macOS most players cannot open an unsigned app without a trip to the system settings.

items.text: The app keeps saves in today’s data folder, so old matches carry over.
items.why: Chosen for saves.

items.text: A full match on macOS as a proof pulls against signing later, because an unsigned Mac app is blocked for most players.
The Mac app ships to players unsigned, with steps to allow it in the system settings.
items.why: Chosen to resolve the Mac proof against signing later.
items.accepted-risk: Most Mac players give up at the block, so the Mac release reaches few players until it is signed.

items.text: The page today shows an engine crash and restarts the engine from the last stoppage with the same score and clock; that works because the engine is a separate process.
The repository has no CI configuration; builds and test runs happen on the owner machine and in WSL.
Direct engine calls in the same program pull against crash recovery, which needs the engine in a separate process.
Direct calls stay; engine errors are caught at the boundary and the match restarts from the last stoppage.
items.why: Chosen for a crash inside the app.
items.accepted-risk: A hard crash, for example running out of memory, still closes the app window.

items.text: Playing the next match without a restart waits for the season layer.
items.why: The season layer changes what the next match is anyway.
items.accepted-risk: Until then, the app plays one match per start and feels like a one-shot launcher.

items.text: Hosted CI comes later; Windows and Linux build locally now, and the Mac waits.
items.why: Chosen for builds.
items.accepted-risk: The Mac proof and the full suite on macOS wait with it.

items.text: The app registers the replay file type, so a double-click on a replay opens it in the app.
items.why: Chosen for replays.

items.text: A season layer design document exists in the realism programme.
CI later with no Mac pulls against the core proofs on all three systems.
The first trial proves the app on Windows and Linux; the macOS proof and the macOS suite runs come with CI or a Mac.
items.why: Windows and Linux can prove the shell now, and there is no Mac and no CI.
items.accepted-risk: Web engine differences on a Mac show up late.
